title: Chain stitch
subtitle: A linked row of loops that builds a broad, flexible outline
excerpt: Chain stitch forms a chain of interlocking loops along any line, giving a bolder, softer outline than back stitch and covering ground quickly when used as a fill.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), chain stitch chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), chain stitch entry.
heroPrompt: Chain stitch line curving along a leaf outline on green linen, dark thread, the loop texture clearly visible, close-up, natural light.

content.text: Chain stitch works by always inserting the needle back through the previous loop, so each new loop holds the one before it open. The chain builds quickly once the rhythm is established and follows curves with ease because each individual loop is short.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 3 to 4 strands for a bold line

content.text: Bring the needle up at point A. Hold the thread in a loop below the line with your thumb.
Insert the needle back at A and bring it up one stitch-length ahead at B, passing through the loop. Pull through gently until the loop forms a rounded oval.
For the next chain: hold the thread in a new loop, insert at B (inside the previous loop), bring up at C. Continue along the line.
To finish the last loop, make one small tacking stitch over its tip rather than beginning a new chain.

items.cause: The thread is pulled to different tensions on each stitch.
items.fix: Pull each loop to the same gentle tension before forming the next one. Consistent finger pressure is the main control.

items.symptom: The chain looks like a series of bumps
items.cause: Stitch length is too short, so the loops crowd together.
items.fix: Aim for loops roughly 4 to 6 mm long.

content.text: Chain stitch is the basis for twisted chain, heavy chain, and cable chain. Worked in tight spiral rows it fills shapes and formed the foundation of traditional tambour beading.
